title: Enterprise Landing Zone (ALZ)
subtitle: Management group hierarchy, policy stacks, and subscription vending for enterprise-scale Azure
summary: The Azure Landing Zone reference implementation establishes a policy-driven governance foundation for enterprise Azure estates. A management group hierarchy scopes compliance policy initiatives across all subscriptions, and subscription vending automates workload onboarding for product teams. Platform, Identity, and Connectivity subscriptions are separated from workload landing zones.
whenToUse: Required for Govern-tier engagements with multiple product teams, regulated workloads, or a dedicated cloud platform team. Do not apply ALZ complexity to a Land-tier single-workload deployment — the governance overhead outweighs the benefit at that scale.
keyDesignDecisions: Management group depth: Platform / Landing Zones / Sandboxes / Decommissioned is the ALZ canonical hierarchy
Policy initiative assignment at management group scope enforces compliance without per-subscription configuration
Subscription vending via Bicep or Terraform module — manual subscription creation is an anti-pattern at this tier
Connectivity subscription hosts the hub VNet, ExpressRoute/VPN gateways, and Azure Firewall (never shared with workloads)
Identity subscription hosts domain controllers, Entra Connect, PKI — isolated from workload blast radius

layers.name: Governance
layers.role: Management group hierarchy, Policy initiative assignments, RBAC role definitions scoped to MG

layers.name: Connectivity Hub
layers.role: Dedicated subscription hosting centralized network appliances for all spoke workloads
services: Azure Virtual WAN or Hub VNet

layers.name: Identity
layers.role: Centralized identity services in a dedicated subscription, isolated from workload blast radius

layers.name: Security & Compliance
layers.role: Continuous compliance posture monitoring and threat detection across all subscriptions

layers.name: Landing Zone Subscriptions
layers.role: Workload subscriptions policy-inherited from management groups, spoke VNets peered to hub

title: N-Tier Web Application
subtitle: Scalable web application with separated presentation, business logic, and data tiers
summary: A classic layered architecture adapted for Azure PaaS: web tier (App Service or Container Apps) handles HTTP traffic behind Application Gateway, business logic tier processes requests, and a managed data tier (Azure SQL, Redis) persists state. Each tier scales independently and is isolated by NSG or Private Endpoints. Availability Zones spread each tier for intra-region redundancy.
whenToUse: Well-understood workloads with clear tier separation — web applications, internal portals, APIs with database backends. Use when the team understands the deployment model and wants predictable operational behavior. Move toward microservices/AKS when the number of independently deployable business capabilities exceeds what a monolith can cleanly support.
keyDesignDecisions: App Service Environments vs. multi-tenant App Service: use ASE only if network injection is required for compliance
Azure SQL Geo-Replication or Auto-Failover Group for RPO/RTO targets below 1 hour
Redis Cache tier: C1 (Standard, 1GB) is the minimum for production HA; Basic has no SLA
Application Gateway v2 with WAF policy is the standard ingress for PCI-scope web applications
Deployment slots (staging → production swap) for zero-downtime releases

layers.name: Edge / Ingress
layers.role: Public traffic inspection, WAF, TLS termination, and global load balancing

layers.name: Web / Presentation Tier
layers.role: Stateless HTTP request handling, session routing, and frontend serving

layers.name: Business Logic Tier
layers.role: API processing, background jobs, and integration with downstream services

layers.name: Data Tier
layers.role: Persistent relational storage, caching layer, and blob/queue storage
services: Azure SQL Database (General Purpose or Business Critical)

layers.name: Identity & Security
layers.role: Managed identity for service-to-service authentication, no credential management

layers.name: Observability
layers.role: End-to-end request tracing, alerting, and availability monitoring

title: AKS Microservices Platform
subtitle: Container orchestration platform for independently deployable microservices with GitOps delivery
summary: A private AKS cluster hosts independently deployable microservices managed by a platform team. Workload Identity replaces pod-level secrets. Node pools are sized and tainted per workload class (system, user, GPU). KEDA and the Cluster Autoscaler handle demand scaling. GitOps via Flux or Argo CD enforces desired state. Azure Container Registry stores and scans images before deployment.
whenToUse: When the number of independently deployable services exceeds what a monolith can cleanly support, when teams need independent release cadences, or when container density economics justify the platform investment. Do not introduce AKS complexity for a single-team application that deploys monthly — App Service is operationally simpler.
keyDesignDecisions: Private cluster: API server accessible only from within the VNet or via approved CIDR ranges
Workload Identity (OIDC + federated credentials) replaces pod-mounted secrets — no credential rotation required
System node pool (Standard_D4s_v5, min 3 nodes across 3 AZs) isolated from user workloads via taint
Azure CNI Overlay or Cilium for pod networking — avoid kubenet in production (no native network policy)
Container image scanning via Microsoft Defender for Containers (admission controller blocks Critical CVEs)
GitOps delivery: Flux v2 or Argo CD reconciles cluster state from a Git repository — no kubectl apply in production

layers.name: Ingress / Service Mesh
layers.role: Cluster-internal L7 routing, mTLS between services, and external traffic admission

layers.name: AKS Cluster
layers.role: Kubernetes control plane and node pools organized by workload class

layers.name: Container Registry & CI/CD
layers.role: Image build, scan, and promotion pipeline feeding GitOps reconciliation
services: Flux v2 or Argo CD (GitOps sync)

layers.name: Data & Messaging
layers.role: Persistent storage and async communication between microservices
services: Azure SQL / Cosmos DB (per-service, not shared)

layers.name: Identity & Secrets
layers.role: Pod-level identity and secret injection without mounting credentials
services: Azure Key Vault (Secrets Store CSI driver)
Azure Container Registry (pull via managed identity)

layers.name: Observability
layers.role: Cluster metrics, container logs, distributed traces, and security events

title: Serverless Event-Driven Architecture
subtitle: Event-triggered compute with durable orchestration for asynchronous workload processing
summary: Azure Functions respond to triggers from Event Grid, Service Bus, or Blob Storage, processing events at scale with no infrastructure management. Durable Functions handle long-running orchestration with checkpoint state in Azure Storage. Event Grid fans out domain events to multiple downstream consumers. The architecture scales to zero — costs are proportional to actual invocations, not provisioned capacity.
whenToUse: Spiky or unpredictable workloads where scale-to-zero economics matter: file processing, webhook handlers, integration pipelines, and async background work. Not suitable for sub-10ms latency requirements (cold start) or stateful streaming workloads where Azure Stream Analytics or Event Hubs with Kafka protocol is more appropriate.
keyDesignDecisions: Consumption Plan for true scale-to-zero economics; Premium Plan required if VNet injection or warm instances are needed
Durable Functions for workflows with checkpoints, fan-out/fan-in, or human approval steps — avoid long-running logic in standard functions
Dead-letter queue (DLQ) on every Service Bus subscription — silent message loss is unacceptable in production
Idempotency: every function must handle duplicate message delivery safely (at-least-once delivery is the default)
Event Grid custom topics for domain events; System topics for native Azure resource events (Blob created, etc.)

layers.name: Event Sources / Triggers
layers.role: Events that initiate function execution — HTTP, timer, storage, messaging, and native Azure resource events

layers.name: Compute
layers.role: Stateless event processors and stateful orchestrators

layers.name: Messaging & Integration
layers.role: Durable async communication, fan-out routing, and retry/DLQ semantics

layers.name: Data & State
layers.role: Durable function state storage, results persistence, and reference data

layers.name: Identity & Security
layers.role: Managed identity for trigger binding authentication, no connection string secrets in code

layers.name: Observability
layers.role: Invocation traces, failure alerts, DLQ monitoring, and orchestration state visibility

title: Multi-Region Active-Passive
subtitle: Cross-region failover architecture for workloads with sub-1-hour RTO requirements
summary: The primary region handles all production traffic. The secondary region is warm-standby: the application is deployed and healthy, data is replicated asynchronously, and traffic failover is automated via Azure Traffic Manager or Azure Front Door. On primary-region failure, Traffic Manager detects the unhealthy endpoint and routes traffic to the secondary within minutes. RTO targets of 15–60 minutes are achievable; sub-15-minute RTO requires active-active.
whenToUse: Workloads with an RTO target between 15 minutes and 4 hours that cannot justify the cost of active-active. Regulated workloads often require documented DR capability with tested failover. Active-passive is the right trade-off when writes are infrequent enough that async replication lag (RPO 1–15 minutes) is acceptable.
keyDesignDecisions: Azure Front Door is preferred over Traffic Manager for HTTP workloads — sub-minute failover vs. 30-second DNS TTL minimum
Azure SQL Auto-Failover Group replicates data asynchronously — measure replication lag under production write load before committing to RPO target
Secondary region App Service / AKS must be deployed and passing health checks before failover — cold secondaries extend RTO unpredictably
DNS-based failover (Traffic Manager) requires application clients to respect TTL — short TTL (30–60s) required
Chaos testing: run a scheduled failover drill quarterly; untested DR plans fail at the worst possible moment

layers.name: Global Traffic Routing
layers.role: Health-check-driven failover between primary and secondary regions
services: Azure Front Door (Priority routing + health probes)

layers.name: Primary Region Compute
layers.role: Active traffic handlers — App Service, AKS, or Container Apps with Availability Zone spread

layers.name: Secondary Region Compute
layers.role: Warm standby — deployed, health-checked, scaled-down until failover
services: Azure App Service (same config as primary, scaled down)
AKS (minimal node count, scales on failover)

layers.name: Data Replication
layers.role: Async replication from primary to secondary — defines the RPO target
services: Azure Cosmos DB (multi-region write or single-write + read replica)
Azure Cache for Redis (geo-replication, Premium tier)

layers.name: Identity & Secrets
layers.role: Cross-region secret availability — Key Vault must be reachable from secondary during outage
services: Azure Key Vault (geo-replicated within region pair)
Microsoft Entra ID (globally available — no DR action needed)

layers.name: Observability & Failover Automation
layers.role: Health monitoring, automated failover trigger, and post-incident analysis

title: Regulated Workload (PCI-DSS / HIPAA)
subtitle: Network segmentation, audit logging, and compliance controls for regulated data environments
summary: Regulated workloads require layered controls that satisfy auditor requirements: a defined cardholder data environment (CDE) or PHI boundary, network segmentation enforced by Azure Firewall and NSGs, comprehensive audit logging shipped to a SIEM, encryption at rest and in transit, and a documented access control model. The architecture scope is intentionally kept minimal — only services that must touch regulated data are in-scope.
whenToUse: Any workload processing, storing, or transmitting cardholder data (PCI-DSS), protected health information (HIPAA), or federal data (FedRAMP). Engage a QSA (PCI) or compliance officer early — architectural decisions made before their review often require expensive redesign. The compliance overlay in this framework's Timeline page includes the additional weeks these reviews add.
keyDesignDecisions: Scope minimization: the smallest possible CDE / PHI boundary is the correct boundary — every additional service adds compliance surface area
All traffic in/out of the regulated boundary transits Azure Firewall — no peering that bypasses the firewall
PCI DSS Requirement 10: logs must be shipped to an immutable, access-controlled SIEM within 24 hours — Sentinel + Log Analytics with WORM retention satisfies this
No standing privileged access: PIM-activated roles, JIT VM access, time-bound access reviews for all in-scope systems
Encryption key management: Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) required for PCI scope data stores; Key Vault HSM-backed keys for highest assurance
Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard provides continuous control assessment — use it as the baseline for audit evidence packages

layers.name: Regulated Boundary (CDE / PHI Zone)
layers.role: Strictly network-segmented zone containing only services that must process regulated data
services: Dedicated VNet (no direct peering to non-regulated)
Azure Policy (deny public endpoints, enforce CMK, require tags)

layers.name: Compute (In-Scope)
layers.role: Compute resources that process regulated data — hardened OS baseline, no public IP
services: Azure App Service (ASE or private endpoint)
Azure Virtual Machines (if required — hardened via Azure Security Benchmark)

layers.name: Data (In-Scope)
layers.role: Data stores holding regulated data — CMK encryption, private endpoints, no public access
services: Azure SQL (Business Critical, CMK, private endpoint)
Azure Blob Storage (CMK, private endpoint, immutable retention)
Azure Key Vault (HSM-backed keys, private endpoint)

layers.name: Access Control
layers.role: No standing access to in-scope systems — all privileged access is time-bound and audited
services: Conditional Access (MFA, compliant device, named location)

layers.name: Audit Logging & SIEM
layers.role: Comprehensive, tamper-evident audit trail for all access and control-plane activity

layers.name: Vulnerability & Posture Management
layers.role: Continuous assessment of misconfigurations, unpatched vulnerabilities, and compliance drift
services: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (CSPM + Regulatory Compliance)
